cards.text: Psalm 148 opens with one word: "Hallelujah!" Then the psalm writer starts calling on everything to praise the LORD. Friend, this is the BIGGEST group invite ever sent, and he is not leaving ANYBODY off the list.

cards.question: Every invite list has to start somewhere. Where does the psalm writer first call for praise to come from?
Up in the heavens, the first ones the psalm writer calls on to praise the LORD are all His ___.

cards.text: After the angels and all His heavenly hosts, he calls out to the lights in the sky: "Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars." He's talking to the SUN, friend, and I talk to my oven every single morning, so who am I to judge?

cards.question: After the sun, moon and stars, the psalm writer is done with the sky. Nothing higher gets called on to praise the LORD.

cards.text: He goes even higher: "Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies." This man is checking the TOP shelf, friend, the one even I can't reach, and I've got a gold base AND a tall hat.

cards.question: Everything up in the heavens is called to praise the name of the LORD. What reason does the psalm writer give?

answers.text: He commanded and they were created
They were made to serve people
They live closest to His throne

cards.question: God doesn't just make the heavens and walk away. He sets them in place to last ___.

cards.text: "He issued a decree that will never pass away." Friend, I shared a junk drawer with an expired coupon for YEARS, so a decree that NEVER runs out sounds like a miracle to me.

cards.question: The heavens got their invite, from the angels all the way up to the highest heavens. Where does the psalm writer call for praise to come from next?

cards.text: He starts at the bottom: all great sea creatures and the ocean depths. Way down in the dark, friend, and they still get called up, and believe me, I KNOW how good that feels.

cards.question: Next on the earth's list is the weather. What does the psalm writer say the powerful wind is doing?

cards.text: Lightning and hail, snow and clouds, the whole forecast gets the invite. The weatherman reads that list and calls it a rough week, friend, but the psalm writer reads it and calls it a CHOIR.

cards.question: On the earth, the psalm writer calls on the mountains and hills to praise the LORD, but the trees don't make the list.

cards.text: Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars, wild animals and all cattle, crawling creatures and flying birds. Friend, if it stands, grows, crawls or flies, it got the invite.

cards.question: After the animals, the psalm writer finally gets to people. Who's at the top of that list?

answers.text: Kings and rulers of the earth

cards.text: Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth. The folks who run the world get the exact same invite as everybody else, friend, and there is NO VIP line.

cards.question: When the psalm writer calls on people to praise the LORD, he calls the old and the young separately, one group at a time.

cards.text: Young men and maidens, old and young together. Same song, same choir, same invite, friend, and it's the best group chat I have EVER been added to.

cards.question: The earth gets the same line the heavens got: "Let them praise the name of the LORD". This time the reason is that His name is the ___ name that is exalted.

cards.text: "His splendor is above the earth and the heavens." Then it gets personal: He has raised up a horn for His people, the praise of all His saints.

cards.question: At the very end, the psalm writer names His people: Israel. How does he describe them?

answers.text: A people sent to the nations

cards.text: And the psalm ends right where it started: "Hallelujah!" He opened with it and closed with it, friend, with all of heaven and earth packed in between like a cookie box filled RIGHT up to the lid.

findings.problem: The opening card says the psalm writer is calling on everything and is "not leaving ANYBODY off the list." That rules out the wrong answer on later true or false cards that ask whether something gets left out. Stop 1 card 5 asks whether nothing higher than the stars gets called on. Stop 2 card 5 asks whether the trees don't make the list. With this setup, both answers are obviously False.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later. Once a choice has been answered, the cards after it can build on that answer. An easy follow-up is fine. For example, once the baker knows the greater light rules the day, a card can ask whether the lesser light rules the night. ... A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Hiding His face" isn't believable as something a powerful wind does. It's a phrase about God, not about weather, so the baker can drop it without thinking. That leaves a two-way pick.

rule.text: Wrong answers for what someone does or says only need to be believable.

findings.problem: This card is almost only verse wording: the v13 quote, then v14 retold close to word for word. The only thing Papa Dorin adds is "Then it gets personal." It has none of his voice, and it gives no help with the moment (a horn raised up for His people). The card reads stripped down.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Nearly every joke uses the same invite comparison. Stop 1 card 1 has "BIGGEST group invite." Stop 1 card 2 has "invite list." Stop 2 card 1 has "got their invite." Stop 2 card 4 has "gets the invite." Stop 2 card 6 has "got the invite." Stop 2 card 8 has "same invite." Stop 2 card 10 has "same invite" and "group chat." The repetition turns into a formula. It also reads pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: No formula. His personality fits whatever moment he's in, whether it's a tense moment in a story, a hard teaching or a quick question. There are no joke quotas and no required kinds of jokes. But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. ... If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
